summary: Cycle 16 observed: 25 of 27 hold; frame-cost (6.14x) and enemies-path (0) contradicted. The cycle refutes the previous cycle's inference: the view-sized wake window gave no saving (matrix as is 417 ms vs the wider window 433; perf worst 6.14x) and the pathing count fell from 5 to 0 with the same level. Both residues are dominated by run-to-run variance of the live fight and the AI, which the loop's single-run probes cannot average out.

claims.text: Correction: cycle 15's 'viewWake 217 ms' was confounded by step order — the matrix measures steps one after another at the same spot, and by that step the fight about the held player had died down (allAsleep, measured after it, read the same 217). This cycle, with the view-sized window installed, asIs read 417 and wideWake 433; the baseline itself read 183 against 133 before. The wake window is not the lever; the frame follows the live fight at the spot.

What holds across both matrix runs: with no enemies the deck is 150 ms (0.82-1.13x of each run's baseline); the set pieces together are ~33 ms (the bridge dressing, not the hills); half resolution changes little; no shader links. With the fight on, the deck reads 2.3-3.5x the baseline within a run, and perf's four spots 4.6-6.1x across cycles.

enemies-path: player held 20.3 game seconds (no deaths, 2 put-backs); movedCount 0 — the hunters in the window were awake and moved (the deck trooper 697, the heavy 475, the road trooper 1553) but away from the bait; the shotgun hunter from 4100, outside the view-sized window, never woke. Cycle 15, same level but for the window, gave 5. The count swings with the AI's choices from run to run.

Put the wake window back to 1700 x 800 (it bought nothing measurable and cost the far hunters), bake, and let the loop re-observe. If frame-cost stays above 1.5x, which every measurement with the fight on says it will, the threshold under the software renderer is the human's decision.

unknowns: How many runs the pathing count needs to be judged fairly (it has read 1, 2, 2, 5, 0).
